# The Pragmatic Method Settles Metaphysical Disputes

The pragmatic method is primarily a method of settling metaphysical disputes that otherwise might be interminable.[^1] Is the world one or many?--fated or free?--material or spiritual?--here are notions either of which may or may not hold good of the world; and disputes over such notions are unending.[^2] The pragmatic method in such cases is to try to interpret each notion by tracing its respective practical consequences.[^3] What difference would it practically make to anyone if this notion rather than that notion were true?[^4] If no practical difference whatever can be traced, then the alternatives mean practically the same thing, and all dispute is idle.[^5] Whenever a dispute is serious, we ought to be able to show some practical difference that must follow from one side or the other's being right.[^6]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "The pragmatic method is primarily a method of settling metaphysical disputes that otherwise might be interminable."
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "Is the world one or many?--fated or free?--material or spiritual?--here are notions either of which may or may not hold good of the world; and disputes over such notions are unending."
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "The pragmatic method in such cases is to try to interpret each notion by tracing its respective practical consequences."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "What difference would it practically make to anyone if this notion rather than that notion were true?"
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "If no practical difference whatever can be traced, then the alternatives mean practically the same thing, and all dispute is idle."
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "Whenever a dispute is serious, we ought to be able to show some practical difference that must follow from one side or the other's being right."
=== FILE: Does the Man Go Round the Squirrel.md ===

# Does the Man Go Round the Squirrel

The corpus of[^1] a ferocious metaphysical dispute[^2] was a squirrel--a live squirrel supposed to be clinging to one side of a tree-trunk; while over against the tree's opposite side a human being was imagined to stand.[^3] This human witness tries to get sight of the squirrel by moving rapidly round the tree, but no matter how fast he goes, the squirrel moves as fast in the opposite direction, and always keeps the tree between himself and the man, so that never a glimpse of him is caught.[^4] The resultant metaphysical problem now is this: DOES THE MAN GO ROUND THE SQUIRREL OR NOT?[^5] Which party is right[^6] depends on what you PRACTICALLY MEAN by 'going round' the squirrel.[^7] If you mean passing from the north of him to the east, then to the south, then to the west, and then to the north of him again, obviously the man does go round him, for he occupies these successive positions.[^8] But if on the contrary you mean being first in front of him, then on the right of him, then behind him, then on his left, and finally in front again, it is quite as obvious that the man fails to go round him, for by the compensating movements the squirrel makes, he keeps his belly turned towards the man all the time, and his back turned away.[^9] Make the distinction, and there is no occasion for any farther dispute.[^10] You are both right and both wrong according as you conceive the verb 'to go round' in one practical fashion or the other.[^11]

[^1]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "The corpus of"
[^2]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "a ferocious metaphysical dispute"
[^3]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "was a squirrel--a live squirrel supposed to be clinging to one side of a tree-trunk; while over against the tree's opposite side a human being was imagined to stand."
[^4]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "This human witness tries to get sight of the squirrel by moving rapidly round the tree, but no matter how fast he goes, the squirrel moves as fast in the opposite direction, and always keeps the tree between himself and the man, so that never a glimpse of him is caught."
[^5]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "The resultant metaphysical problem now is this: DOES THE MAN GO ROUND THE SQUIRREL OR NOT?"
[^6]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "Which party is right"
[^7]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "depends on what you PRACTICALLY MEAN by 'going round' the squirrel."
[^8]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "If you mean passing from the north of him to the east, then to the south, then to the west, and then to the north of him again, obviously the man does go round him, for he occupies these successive positions."
[^9]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "But if on the contrary you mean being first in front of him, then on the right of him, then behind him, then on his left, and finally in front again, it is quite as obvious that the man fails to go round him, for by the compensating movements the squirrel makes, he keeps his belly turned towards the man all the time, and his back turned away."
[^10]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "Make the distinction, and there is no occasion for any farther dispute."
[^11]: [[Pragmatism - Lecture II - What Pragmatism Means#What Pragmatism Means]] "You are both right and both wrong according as you conceive the verb 'to go round' in one practical fashion or the other."
